name: Accessibility settings inferred
plain: Combining contrast, motion, forced colors, zoom and font size to guess a disability.
meaning: No single API says disabled, but together prefers-contrast, forced-colors, reduced-motion, large fonts and zoom flag vision, vestibular or motor needs. Under GDPR or similar this may be special-category data.

web.api: Combination of CSS media queries, zoom and font size

access.persistence: read fresh on every page load; nothing stored
access.iframe: Readable from cross-origin iframes too (same values)

fields.name: signals combined
fields.range: forced-colors, prefers-contrast, prefers-reduced-motion, inverted-colors, zoom, font size

limits.headline: Can guess you may use accessibility settings by combining several browser signals
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens quietly while the page loads and you use it
can: Check settings such as high contrast, reduced motion, forced colors, zoom and large text
Guess you may have low vision or need less motion when several signals line up
Change the page design to fit those settings
cannot: Learn for sure that you have a disability
See your medical details or assistive tech by name
Rely on one signal alone; it takes several together

story.what_it_is: Sites can guess a disability from your zoom, contrast, motion and font settings.

marketing.name: prefers-reduced-motion
marketing.pitch: Google teaches pages to honor the person's reduced motion setting so animations can be turned down.

story.for_you: You never see anything. If you use high contrast, large text, big zoom or reduced motion, a site can notice. These settings help you read, but together they can hint at a health or vision condition.
story.for_makers: Makers use these settings to adapt the page for the person, which is the good use. Trackers and ad systems can use the same signals as a clue about health or age, which is sensitive and a privacy risk.

use_cases.example: A site switches to a calmer layout without animation when it sees reduced motion is on.
A browser game turns off screen shake and flashing when it sees reduced motion, and uses stronger contrast colors.
A video site turns on captions and larger controls when contrast and zoom settings suggest low vision.
An ad profile quietly adds 'may have low vision' as a hidden clue to target products, which is a privacy concern.
A fingerprint script uses font size, zoom and contrast as part of a unique ID.
A fraud tool treats odd combinations as a sign of automation or a spoofed browser.

technical_bounds: Only probabilistic; screen reader use is not directly detectable

linkedin.how: BrowserGate alleges extension scan infers disability and neurodivergence; separate from media queries.
